source.title: The Impact of Depth on Compositional Generalization in Transformer Language Models
source.authors: Jackson Petty; Sjoerd van Steenkiste; Ishita Dasgupta; F. Sha; Dan Garrette; Tal Linzen

record.tranche_reason: Tests whether language-model validation perplexity is sensitive to architecture shape using a controlled depth–width trade-off at fixed parameter count, rather than testing the original scaling-law sweeps.
record.gate_note: The study varies depth and feed-forward width at fixed parameter counts and reports C4 validation perplexity. It does not fit power laws, vary parameter count, token count or compute as scaling variables, or predict larger runs from smaller ones. Compositional-generalization results are not rows for the listed versions: those experiments vary depth at fixed parameter count, not scale or pretraining loss.
record.test_reason: The study holds parameter count fixed (41M, 134M, 374M) and trades depth against feed-forward width. It reports C4 validation perplexity for each shape, which bears directly on V4. It fits no power laws and does not vary scale as a scaling variable, so V1–V3 and V5–V7 are not tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct, but incomplete. The authors' main conclusion concerns compositional generalization: at fixed parameter count, deeper models generalize better after fine-tuning, with rapidly diminishing returns, and this is not explained by lower pretraining perplexity alone. On language modeling, deeper models reach lower perplexity with diminishing returns, and performance degrades when d_ff falls below d_model. Because latency is linear in depth, they recommend shallower models than is typical for a fixed parameter budget.
record.recipe_differences: Rather than sweep parameters, tokens or compute and fit loss laws, the study holds total parameter count fixed and varies depth against feed-forward width. Models are pretrained on C4 for 1M steps, roughly 131B tokens.
record.method_sensitivity: Validation perplexity changes with depth and the corresponding feed-forward width; the point where performance worsens varies across parameter classes.

fits_no_version.finding: At fixed parameter count, deeper models fine-tuned on COGS, COGS-vf, GeoQuery and English passivization generalize more compositionally. The benefit saturates after a few layers and persists when pretraining perplexity is matched.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Depth, independent of parameter count, affects compositional generalization after fine-tuning beyond what pretraining loss predicts.

fits_no_version.finding: Training latency grows linearly with depth at fixed parameter count (Figure 8).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Shape affects compute or latency cost at fixed parameters even when loss is nearly unchanged.

record.peer_reviewed: North American Chapter of the Association for Computational Linguistics
record.problems: Table 3 reports one run per condition. Figure 2 reports means over 5 runs with error bars, but the table's individual values are single-run results.
record.rows_left_out: No C4 validation-perplexity rows from Table 3 were left out. The compositional-generalization task results were not extracted because they do not measure a listed claim version.

untested.parts: Only the feed-forward width vs depth trade-off with d_model and d_attn fixed. Not tested: d_model/n_layer aspect ratio as in Kaplan, attention heads, or other architecture details. All values are single runs at 1M steps on C4.

missing.what: Feed-forward-ratio analysis: perplexity worsens once d_ff < d_model. The near-optimal ratio range is narrow at 41M and widens with model size, so small models are more shape-sensitive (no numeric values).
Mean perplexity over 5 runs with error bars per depth and size class. These are the replicated values behind the single-run Table 3.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's 'challenges' label for 1-layer models is downgraded to limits_scope. V4 claims near-invariance only 'within a wide range', and 1-layer models of width 512–1024 lie outside Kaplan's tested aspect ratios. The extreme-shallow penalty therefore bounds that range rather than contradicting it. The narrow-end rows R07 and R26 show only 2–3% penalties and are moved to supports. Kaplan varied d_model/n_layer with a fixed ff ratio, whereas this study varies d_ff with d_model fixed, so the shape axis differs from the original.

versions.untested_parts: Power-law loss as a function of parameter count, tokens or compute.
Extrapolating loss from small runs to much larger runs.
Compute-optimal parameter and token allocation as compute changes.
Tests depth and feed-forward width at fixed parameter count; does not broadly vary other architecture details.
Predictability of downstream performance from scale or pretraining loss.
Dependence of fitted scaling exponents or compute-optimal allocations on fitting and setup choices.

source_check.label: supports
source_check.condition: Intermediate depths within each size class: 41M at 3–7 layers, 134M at 6–26 layers, 374M at 6–32 layers
source_check.reason: Table 3 shows perplexities within approximately 0–5.6% of each class minimum over these ranges (R03–R07, R11–R16, R21–R26), consistent with modest shape effects.

relationships.condition: Very shallow, very wide models (1–2 layers; 4 layers at 374M) and the very narrow 134M 32-layer model
relationships.reason: 1-layer models are 1.59–1.99x the best perplexity and 2-layer models 8–29% worse. The penalty grows with model size, so the near-invariant range is bounded and size-dependent (R01, R02, R08, R09, R17, R18, R19, R20).
relationships.display_finding: Single-layer models reached 1.59–1.99 times the best perplexity and two-layer models were 8–29% worse, with larger penalties at larger model sizes.

tranche.reason: Trades depth against feed-forward width while holding embedding and attention dimensions fixed within each parameter class; directly examines the shape-insensitivity question using a different architectural sweep.

source_check.notes:
Table 3 reports single runs; Figure 2 reports means and error bars over five runs. The text states a 374M single-layer ratio of 1.99, whereas Table 3 gives 28.4/14.4 ≈ 1.97.
The claim that V6 is untested is too broad: Section 3.3/Figure 6 also shows depth-dependent compositional generalization at matched pretraining perplexity.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Models near the best-performing depth within each parameter class
reader_labels.reason: Several tested depths have validation perplexity close to the class best, consistent with modest shape effects in that range (R03-R07, R10-R16, R21-R26).

reader_labels.label: challenges
reader_labels.condition: Single-layer models in all three parameter classes
reader_labels.reason: The single-layer models have much higher perplexity than the best models in their classes; the reported ratios are 1.59, 1.86 and 1.99 (R01, R08, R18).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Very deep, narrow models and the range of shapes that remain near-optimal
reader_labels.reason: Perplexity can worsen at the narrow end, and the authors say the near-optimal feed-forward-ratio range varies with model size (R07, R17, R26).
